- Key clinical features: adolescent (16 y), slowly enlarging firm-to-hard, well-circumscribed 6 × 6 cm protuberant red “bullalike” tumor on upper arm over 6 months, no LAD, otherwise well.
- Gross pathology: multilocular spaces beneath epidermis and a deep dermal solid tumor with chalky-white cut surface and lobulated appearance — chalky-white/calcified cut surface is characteristic of a calcifying adnexal lesion.
- Histology: basophilic cells and shadow (ghost) cells in the deep dermis are classic for pilomatricoma (pilomatrixoma, formerly calcifying epithelioma of Malherbe). The overlying dilated lymphatic vessels explain the bullous/lymphangiectatic clinical appearance (bullous pilomatricoma is a described variant).
- Clinicopathologic concordance strongly supports pilomatrixoma (giant/bullous variant) as the top diagnosis.
- Alternative diagnoses considered (less likely because they lack the pathognomonic shadow/ghost cells or the typical calcified nodular core): epidermal inclusion (epidermoid) cyst with calcification, pilar (trichilemmal) cyst, pilomatrical carcinoma/malignant pilomatrixoma (rare; would show atypia/invasion), and cystic lymphatic malformation/lymphangioma producing bullous change.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Pilomatricoma (pilomatrixoma; calcifying epithelioma of Malherbe) — giant/bullous variant (most likely)
2. Epidermal inclusion (epidermoid) cyst with secondary calcification/rupture and overlying lymphatic dilation
3. Pilar (trichilemmal) cyst with calcification/ossification
4. Pilomatrical carcinoma (malignant pilomatrixoma) — rare, consider if atypia/invasion present
5. Cystic lymphatic malformation / lymphangioma with secondary reaction around a calcified dermal lesion
